topics.name: Heat, work, and the laws of thermodynamics

guide.title: Thermodynamics: review guide
guide.intro: Thermodynamics connects the motion of huge numbers of molecules to quantities you can measure: pressure, temperature, and volume. It tracks energy entering and leaving a gas as heat and work, and it explains why heat flows from hot to cold.
guide.equationNote: Constants used in this unit: R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K. Gas laws use absolute temperature in kelvins: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.

sections.title: Pressure, temperature, and the ideal gas law
body: Pressure is force per area, P = F/A, measured in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). A gas presses outward on every surface it touches.

For an ideal gas, PV = nRT = Nk_BT. In a sealed container (fixed amount of gas), PV/T stays constant, so heating a gas at constant volume raises its pressure in proportion to its absolute temperature.
points: Always use kelvins in gas laws; a ratio of Celsius temperatures gives wrong answers.
Two objects in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature, and no net energy flows between them.
Constant volume: P ∝ T. Constant pressure: V ∝ T. Constant temperature: P ∝ 1/V.

sections.title: Kinetic theory: molecules and collisions
body: A gas's pressure comes from molecules colliding with the walls. Each collision changes a molecule's momentum, so the wall exerts a force on the molecule, and by Newton's third law the molecule pushes on the wall.
Temperature measures the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules: K_avg = (3/2)k_BT. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster on average.
points: v_rms = √(3k_BT/m), so doubling the speed takes four times the absolute temperature.
Individual molecules have a spread of speeds; temperature describes the average.
Different gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy per molecule, not the same speed.
equations: average translational kinetic energy per molecule

sections.title: Heat, work, and the laws of thermodynamics
body: A thermodynamic system is the part of the world you track, such as a gas in a cylinder; everything else is its surroundings. Its internal energy U is the total kinetic and potential energy of its molecules; for an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature.

First law: ΔU = Q + W, where Q is the heat added to the system and W is the work done on the system. An expanding gas does work on its surroundings, so the work done on it is negative. On a PV diagram, the area under the path is the size of the work.
points: Constant pressure: W = −PΔV. Isothermal (ideal gas): ΔU = 0, so Q = −W. Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = W.
Energy moves as heat by conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction through a slab: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L.
Second law: the total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. Heat flows from hot to cold on its own because spreading energy out evenly is overwhelmingly more probable than the reverse.
equations: first law (W is the work done on the system)
work done on a gas at constant pressure

example.prompt: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 800 J of heat while expanding at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 0.0020 m³ to 0.0050 m³. Find the work done on the gas and its change in internal energy.

misconceptions: “Temperature and heat are the same thing.”
Temperature describes the average kinetic energy of molecules; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
“A gas that expands has work done on it.”
An expanding gas does work on its surroundings, so the work done on it is negative.
Gas laws need absolute temperature in kelvins.
Same temperature means the same average kinetic energy; lighter molecules move faster.

questions.prompt: A gas pushes on a piston of area 0.020 m² with a force of 3000 N. What pressure does the gas exert on the piston?
choiceExplanations: 60 Pa multiplies the force by the area; pressure divides the force by the area.
6.7 × 10⁻⁶ Pa divides the area by the force: the ratio is upside down.
3000 N is the force; it still has to be divided by the area.

questions.prompt: A sealed, rigid container holds gas at 27 °C and 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa. The gas is heated to 177 °C. What is its new pressure?
questions.explanation: The volume and amount of gas are fixed, so P ∝ T in kelvins. T goes from 300 K to 450 K, so P = 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa × 450/300 = 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa.
choiceExplanations: 7.9 × 10⁵ Pa uses the Celsius ratio 177/27; gas laws need kelvins.
0.80 × 10⁵ Pa uses the inverse ratio 300/450, as if pressure fell when the gas was heated.
The container is rigid, so the volume cannot change; the pressure must rise as the temperature rises.

questions.prompt: A gas occupies 0.050 m³ at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 400 K. About how many moles of gas are there? (R = 8.31 J/(mol·K))
choiceExplanations: 0.33 mol is RT/(PV), the ratio upside down.
25 mol is PV/T; the gas constant R was left out.
1200 mol is PV/R; the temperature was left out.

questions.prompt: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas doubles. What happens to the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules?
choices: It increases by a factor of √2
questions.explanation: K_avg = (3/2)k_BT is proportional to the absolute temperature, so doubling T doubles K_avg.
choiceExplanations: Kinetic energy is proportional to T itself, not to T².
√2 is the factor for the rms speed, which goes as √T; the kinetic energy goes as T.
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy, so a higher temperature means more kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: The absolute temperature of a gas is multiplied by 4. By what factor does the root-mean-square speed of its molecules change?
questions.explanation: v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) is proportional to √T, so multiplying T by 4 multiplies v_rms by √4 = 2.
choiceExplanations: 4 is the factor for the average kinetic energy; speed goes as the square root of T.
16 squares the factor instead of taking its square root.
Molecules move faster at higher temperature, so the speed must increase.

questions.prompt: Helium (molar mass 4 g/mol) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g/mol) are at the same temperature. What is the ratio of the rms speed of helium molecules to that of oxygen molecules?
questions.explanation: At the same temperature both gases have the same average kinetic energy, so v_rms ∝ 1/√m. The ratio is √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.8: helium molecules move faster.
choiceExplanations: 8 is the mass ratio; speed depends on the square root of the mass ratio.
Equal temperature means equal average kinetic energy, not equal speed; the lighter molecules move faster.
About 0.35 is √(4/32), which would make the lighter helium molecules slower.

questions.prompt: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
choices: Molecules collide with the walls; each collision changes a molecule's momentum, so the molecules push on the walls
Gravity pulls the gas molecules down onto the walls
The molecules repel the walls electrically without touching them
Heat pushes outward on the walls even when the molecules are not moving
questions.explanation: When a molecule bounces off a wall, its momentum changes, so the wall exerts a force on it. By Newton's third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Many collisions per second add up to a steady pressure.
choiceExplanations: Gas pressure acts equally on the top, sides, and bottom of a container, which gravity alone cannot explain.
In kinetic theory the force comes from collisions, not from forces acting across a distance.
Heat is energy in transfer, not a push; the pressure comes from moving molecules hitting the walls.

questions.prompt: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in the gas's internal energy?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q + W, where W is the work done on the gas. The gas does 200 J of work, so W = −200 J and ΔU = 500 J − 200 J = +300 J.
choiceExplanations: +700 J adds the work instead of subtracting it; doing work on the surroundings takes energy out of the gas.
−300 J has both signs reversed: the gas gains more energy as heat than it gives up as work.
+500 J ignores the 200 J of energy the gas gives up by doing work.

questions.prompt: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 0.010 m³ to 0.030 m³. How much work is done on the gas?
questions.explanation: W = −PΔV = −(2.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(0.020 m³) = −4000 J. The gas does 4000 J of work on its surroundings as it expands.
choiceExplanations: +4000 J is the work done by the gas; the work done on an expanding gas is negative.
−6000 J uses the final volume, 0.030 m³, instead of the change in volume, 0.020 m³.
Work is done whenever the volume changes against a pressure; only a constant volume gives zero work.

questions.prompt: Heat is conducted through a flat slab. A second slab of the same material is twice as thick and has twice the area, with the same temperature difference across it. How does its rate of heat flow compare?
choices: It is four times as large
questions.explanation: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L. Doubling A doubles the rate and doubling L halves it, so the two changes cancel.
choiceExplanations: Doubling the area alone would double the rate, but the doubled thickness halves it again.
Doubling the thickness alone would halve the rate, but the doubled area doubles it again.
Thickness is in the denominator, so increasing it reduces the rate rather than increasing it.

questions.prompt: A hot block and a cold block are placed in contact inside an insulated box. Which statement is true as they reach thermal equilibrium?
choices: Energy flows from the hot block to the cold block until their temperatures are equal, and the total entropy increases
The total entropy stays the same, because energy is conserved
Energy flows from the cold block to the hot block until their temperatures are equal
At equilibrium the two blocks must have equal internal energies
questions.explanation: Heat flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature. The entropy the cold block gains is larger than the entropy the hot block loses, so the total entropy of the isolated system increases until the temperatures are equal.
choiceExplanations: Energy is conserved, but entropy is not: the second law says it increases in a spontaneous process like this.
Heat does not flow on its own from a colder object to a hotter one.
Thermal equilibrium means equal temperatures; blocks of different sizes or materials can have different internal energies.

questions.prompt: An ideal gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature. Which statement is true?
choices: Its internal energy does not change, so it gives off heat equal to the work done on it
Its internal energy increases by the work done on it
No heat is exchanged, because the temperature is constant
Its temperature rises, because work is done on it
questions.explanation: For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature, so at constant temperature ΔU = 0. The first law, 0 = Q + W, then gives Q = −W: the gas releases as heat exactly the energy it receives as work.
choiceExplanations: That would be true if no heat could leave (an adiabatic process); here the temperature, and so U, stays fixed.
Constant temperature does not mean no heat; heat must leave to keep the temperature from rising.
The process is at constant temperature by definition; the energy from the work leaves as heat.
